title: Edge handshake: tail-trade benchmark collateral (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working collateral draft summarizing a lightweight benchmark that compares handshake/warmup penalties and tail-latency cost tradeoffs when routing to edge-proximate fast-paths versus core pooled capacity. Intended audience: console/product PMs, runtime engineers, and solutions. Not final — experimental notes, ascii charts, and next-steps included.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Small interactive requests (2–8 tokens of user prompt + 20–60 token responses) show dominant cost from handshake overhead when requests are routed cold to dedicated edge warmers.
- Pre-warming a small fast-path pool at edge reduces p99 by ~40–55ms and total per-query cost by 6–12% for our median microburst patterns, but increases baseline idle GPU minutes (monthly commit) cost.
- For sporadic microbursts (<50 qps peaks lasting <15s across many edge nodes) the most cost-effective strategy is a hybrid: small edge warmers + on-demand core fallback with a conservative 200ms fast-path timeout.

Experiment setup (concise):
- Model: open-7b-like transformer (baseline config used in infra lab).
- Decoding: sampling, typical response length 48 tokens, decode top-k 40.
- Hardware: edge node: 1x A10s-like GPU (small node proxy for multi-tenant edge pool), core: 1x A100-80GB (pooled, higher throughput).
- Networking: simulated regional RTT: edge 8ms median, core 32ms median.
- Handshake cost components measured separately: TLS + auth + container spin-up + kernel cold path = baseline handshake.
- Workloads: three microburst shapes (needle, short-train, sustained) each driven by Poisson arrival within burst window.
- Cost metric: amortized dollars-per-query (including idle amortization for pre-warm minutes) + observed p50/p95/p99 latency.

Key numeric results (ASCII table):
- Columns: scenario | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | $/query (amortized) | notes

needle (cold-to-edge)       | 96   | 232  | 398  | $0.0034 | high p99 from handshake spikes
needle (prewarm-edge small)  | 58   | 110  | 170  | $0.0031 | small per-query saving, idle cost visible
needle (core fallback)       | 104  | 190  | 260  | $0.0029 | slightly higher p50, lower $/query due to better GPU efficiency
short-train (hybrid 2min)   | 72   | 135  | 205  | $0.00305| hybrid with 200ms fast-path timeout
sustained (core-only)       | 90   | 125  | 170  | $0.0026 | best $/query at sustained high qps

Interpretation notes: 
- p99 is handshake-dominated in cold-to-edge scenario: the distribution has long tail events when container and kernel paths cold-start together.
- Core pooled resources have lower per-token unit cost (better throughput) but lose on tail for short bursts because network RTT adds 20–40ms.
- Prewarming edge nodes improves p95/p99 significantly but the total monthly cost impact depends on idle occupancy: at 30% utilization prewarm is cost-neutral; below ~12% utilization prewarm hurts unit economics.

Microtrace sketch (typical cold handshake path):
- t0: client sends request (8ms RTT)
- t8: ingress accepts, token accounting & auth (4–12ms), route selection
- t20: allocate container slot + load kernels (40–200ms variable)
- t220: model warm, first token decode (20–40ms)
- observed p99 aligns with kernel load tail (most variable bucket)

Breakdown of cost drivers (rough):
- kernel/container cold path: 55% of additional tail latency events
- TLS/auth + routing: 10–15%
- network RTT amplification: 15–20%
- decode time: remainder (depends on token count)

Cost sensitivity sketch (textual):
- Idle prewarm minutes cost assumptions: $0.40/gpu-hour (edge amortization).
- Per-token execution cost (core optimized): $0.0008 per 100 tokens.
- Under needle bursts (~6 qps for 7s) prewarm reduces p99 at an expense of ~0.02–0.06 $/hour in baseline idle cost per edge node. For fleets of many small nodes this multiplies quickly.

Decision heuristics (draft):
- If median edge node utilization (over business hours) > 20% -> maintain a small prewarm pool sized to absorb 95th percentile of microburst concurrency.
- If bursts are extremely short (<10s) and rare -> rely on core fallback + adaptive client-side retry/backoff; do not prewarm globally.
- Implement a 200–300ms fast-path timeout: keep requests on edge fast-path if handshake not completed inside timeout, then fallback to core; this empirically recovers both p99 and $/query in mixed traffic.

Visual ASCII: latency vs time sample (needle scenario):
Time(ms) | 0    50   100  150  200  250  300  400
Cold-edge| 8    20   68   140  220  300  360  420
Prewarm  | 8    20   50   62   72   90   120  150
Core     | 32   56   80   110  150  200  230  260

Operational risks and caveats: 
- Multi-tenant edge nodes have less predictable kernel initialization times than dedicated nodes; our bench used synthetic isolation which may understate variance.
- Network jitter at customers' regional ISPs can add 10–30ms unpredictably, particularly in APAC.
- Cost figures are approximate; need to reconcile with finance unit rates before shipping recommendations.

Actionable next steps (for follow-up experiments):
1) Run a variant with H100-like core and GPU sharing factor to quantify kernel eviction vs reuse in container pools. (Owner: Ibrahim)
2) Prototype 200ms fast-path timeout rule in runtime and measure client-observed p99 over multi-day traces. (Owner: Lena)
3) Simulate fleet-level economics with fleet size 500–2000 edge nodes to determine threshold utilization where prewarm becomes net positive. (Owner: Tom)
4) Capture stack-level microtraces for cold kernel initialization to identify the heavy tail component (syscalls, disk IO, or model weight paging).

Appendix: raw microburst parameters used in runs (for reproducibility):
- needle: burst_duration=7s, lambda_peak=6 qps, baseline=0.2 qps
- short-train: burst_duration=45s, lambda_peak=3 qps, baseline=0.5 qps
- sustained: burst_duration=600s, lambda_peak=12 qps, baseline=2 qps
- random seed: 2029-02-01-EDGE-BENCH

Notes to reviewers: 
- This doc is intentionally compact. If actionable, we should convert to a one-pager for Console collateral with two small charts (p99 vs $/query vs prewarm size) and a short recommendations box.
- Please add missing linked artifacts (traces or PRs) to the linked_artifacts list above.
summary: Draft benchmark collateral comparing edge prewarm vs core fallback for microbursts; includes ascii tables, interpretation, and next steps.
